New restrictions on inverters from countries considered as high-risk by the European Commission, including China, could affect the outlook for solar PV and energy storage projects across Europe, bringing questions on impacts on equipment availability, established sales and aftersales infrastructure, project costs and ultimately development timelines. 
Chinese suppliers accounted for more than 80% of European inverter shipments in 2025. For utilities and developers looking to alternative suppliers, higher costs and limited availability could put further pressure on already-tight project economics, despite growing available supply from Western manufacturers.

How could inverter restrictions affect solar and storage projects? 
The impact will vary significantly by market and project type. Central and Eastern Europe is particularly exposed, while utility-scale solar and energy storage projects could face procurement challenges as developers look beyond established Chinese suppliers.  
Rising equipment costs and supply constraints could also have wider implications for project economics, commissioning timelines and the viability of planned capacity.

What could current and potential inverter rules mean for future deployments across EU markets? 
For solar and energy storage developers, EPCs and wholesalers, understanding the implications goes beyond inverter procurement. Changing supplier requirements could influence project economics, development risk and ultimately how much planned solar and storage capacity is delivered.
